---
title: "Early and Late Complications of Liver Transplantation"
format: revealjs
---


## Evolution of Liver Transplantation

- Liver transplantation (LT) has evolved from a high-risk procedure to a standard treatment for liver failure.
- Significant morbidity and mortality historically.
- 1-year survival rates exceed 85%.
- 5-year survival rates exceed 70%.
- Despite improvements, life-threatening complications still occur, sometimes requiring reoperation.

## Shifting Demographics: Hepatitis C to NASH

- Hepatitis C cirrhosis was historically the main indication for LT in Europe and North America.
- Effective antiviral therapy has changed this landscape.
- Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) is quickly becoming the most common indication.
- Rapid increase in NASH resulting in decompensated liver failure.

## The NASH Epidemic

- Expected to surpass effectively treated viral hepatitis.
- Anticipated increase in end-stage liver disease (ESLD) related deaths by 178% by 2030.
- Shifts the demographic profile of transplant recipients.

## Obesity Epidemic: Impact on Donors

- 2-fold effect impacting LT complications.
- First effect: Increasing the demand for livers.
- Second effect: Increasing prevalence of fatty liver disease in potential organ donors.
- Increased number of discarded livers from brain-dead donors.
- Increased number of transplanted grafts with higher degrees of macrosteatosis.

## Obesity Epidemic: Macrosteatosis Risks

- Survival rates with macrosteatosis greater than 30% are comparable to less fatty livers.
- However, postoperative complication rates are markedly increased:
  - Postreperfusion syndrome (PRS)
  - Early allograft dysfunction (EAD)
  - Postoperative dialysis
  - Need for a second operation

## Obesity Epidemic: Impact on Recipients

- LT recipients have a higher frequency of obesity.
- Body mass index (BMI) greater than 30 is associated with:
  - Increased rate of postoperative cardiopulmonary complications.
  - Longer intensive care unit (ICU) stays.

## Marginal Donors and Surgical Expertise

- As expertise grows, surgeons perform LT on patients previously considered poor candidates.
- Increased use of marginal donor livers.
- Surgical techniques to increase donor pool:
  - Reduced-size grafts
  - Split-liver grafts

## Living-Donor Liver Transplantation (LDLT) Complications

- Parenchymal-splitting operations bring unique complications.
- Incidence of hepatic artery thrombosis (HAT), bile leaks, and stricture is at least two times higher in living-donor grafts vs cadaveric grafts.
- Learning curve exists to reduce these complications.

## Small-for-Size Syndrome (SFSS)

- Major complication after LDLT.
- Characterized by:
  - Hyperbilirubinemia
  - Coagulopathy
  - Encephalopathy observed shortly after transplant.

## SFSS vs Early Allograft Dysfunction (EAD)

- SFSS terminology is becoming historic.
- EAD is a more appropriate term to describe graft dysfunction.
- Graft size is not the only factor for slow return of hepatic function in LDLT and cadaveric donors.
- Despite higher morbidity in LDLT, patient and graft survival are similar or superior to deceased donors.

## Procurement: Team Dispatch

- Process begins with identifying a suitable organ.
- Procurement teams are dispatched for recovery.
- Liver procurement team dictates dissection below the diaphragm.
- Cardiac and thoracic teams work in concert for heart/lungs.
- Careful planning required to minimize cold-ischemia time for heart and lungs.

## Brain Death and Cardiac Instability

- Ideal conditions: orderly and well-controlled operation.
- Reality: Patient progressing to brain death rapidly can show cardiac instability.
- Can result in expedited operation.
- Perfusion cannulae hastily placed.
- Identification of appropriate anatomy is difficult; technical errors more likely.

## Donation After Cardiac Death (DCD)

- Gained popularity since the 1990s to increase organ availability.
- Estimated to increase donor pool by 10% in 2010.
- UNOS data: DCD donors increased from 6% to 11% of all donors (2010 to 2019).
- Patient deemed hopeless but not "brain dead" is allowed to die naturally after removal of supportive measures.
- Organs procured after 2 to 5 minutes of asystole.

## DCD Outcomes and Ischemic Cholangiopathy

- DCD outcomes are mixed but generally acceptable.
- Concerns for increased biliary strictures and worse long-term graft survival.
- Modern assessment supports comparable outcomes to brain-dead donors with appropriate selection.
- Ischemic cholangiopathy is a major feared complication.

## Normothermic Perfusion

- Use of normothermic regional perfusion and normothermic machine perfusion.
- Believed to make ischemic cholangiopathy much less common.
- Expands the usable donor pool safely.

## Procurement Injuries Overview

- Injuries during liver procurement occur in roughly 20% to 30% of organ donors.
- Broken down into:
  - Parenchymal injuries
  - Vascular injuries
  - Bile duct injuries

## Aberrant Hepatic Artery Ligation

- Most common major injury during liver procurement.
- Occurs by failure to recognize replaced/accessory right or left hepatic artery during hilar dissection.
- Or unintentional division during organ removal.

## Hiatt et al. Data on Arterial Anatomy

- 1000 donor case series:
  - Replaced/accessory right hepatic artery in roughly 10% of donors.
  - Similar frequency for left replaced/accessory arteries.
  - 3% had dual replacement arteries.
- Hilum-replaced left and right arteries represent two-thirds of all vascular injuries during procurement.

## Consequences of Arterial Injuries

- Serious because segments of the liver are not perfused during recovery.
- Usually require reconstruction on the back table before reimplantation.
- Associated with a high rate of early HAT (30%).
- Subsequent need for re-transplantation.

## Parenchymal Injuries

- Most common form of minor liver injury during graft removal.
- Can also occur during graft implantation.
- Treated with topical hemostatics, cautery, or liver stitch.
- Associated with long operative times and increased blood loss.
- Do not have an impact on long-term graft function.

## Bile Duct Injuries

- More infrequent complication.
- Can be caused by stripping vascular supply or cutting the duct too short.
- Managed by Roux-en-Y biliary reconstruction.
- Typically not associated with graft loss.

## Cold-Ischemia and Macrosteatosis

- Prolonged cold-ischemia time contributes to recipient morbidity.
- Grafts with more than 12 hours of cold ischemia are at increased risk for graft loss and complications.
- Macrosteatosis greater than 30% is associated with poor early graft function.

## High BMI Donors

- Used less commonly for liver grafts.
- Bedside and procurement biopsy can help improve utilization without increased risk.
- Confirms percent of macrosteatosis.
- Macrosteatosis greater than 30% is only prevalent in 21% of high BMI donors.
- Majority of these donors can be used for LT.

## En Bloc Procurement Method

- Visceral adipose tissue makes procurement challenging and time-consuming.
- To minimize dissection-related injuries, some suggest the en bloc method.
- Removal of abdominal organs with back-table dissection after procurement.
- Attention to detail and identification of appropriate anatomy helps avoid injury.

## Coagulopathy in ESLD

- Patients with ESLD present with a spectrum of coagulation abnormalities.
- Combination of pro and anticoagulants with derangements of fibrinolysis.
- Prone to both massive hemorrhage and life-threatening thrombosis.
- Compounded by portal hypertension and adhesions from prior surgery.

## Portal HTN and Adhesions

- Previous operations increase risk.
- Prolonged lysis of adhesions increases operation duration.
- Creates additional raw surface areas for bleeding.
- Leads to derangements in temperature and fluid homeostasis.
- Worsens coagulopathy, creating a vicious cycle.

## Preoperative Assessment

- Guides anesthesia and surgical team for massive bleeding risk.
- Attenuating blood loss improves long-term outcomes.
- Blood loss has incremental increase in postoperative complications and decrease in graft survival.

## Historical Blood Utilization

- LT historically had a reputation for draining blood banks.
- Early report from 1980s: 3% to 9% of all blood products in Pittsburgh central blood bank used for LT.
- Proposed threshold for excessive bleeding: more than 10 units of red blood cells (RBCs).

## Viscoelastic Testing (TEG and ROTEM)

- Used to predict massive transfusion.
- TEG maximum amplitude associated with massive transfusion (higher performance than INR and MELD).
- ROTEM outperforms conventional assays in predicting nonsurgical bleeding after LT.

## Preemptive Coagulopathy Treatment

- Often not indicated for mild to moderate derangements.
- Platelets believed to be rapidly sequestered by the spleen.
- Plasma transfusions can exacerbate venous hypertension and paradoxically increase bleeding.

## Prothrombin Complex Concentrate (PCC)

- Early use associated with reduced blood loss during LT.
- Corrects INR without requiring the volume of plasma.
- Associated with life-threatening thrombotic complications.
- Conservative use advised until ongoing clinical trial results are released.

## Hypercoagulable Profile in Cirrhosis

- Evolving measurements show a cohort of LT recipients present with hypercoagulable profiles.
- Cirrhosis is an independent risk factor for deep vein thrombosis (DVT).
- NASH is associated with an even higher risk of thrombotic complications.
- Conventional measurements do not capture this state.

## TEG and HAT Risk

- Elevated preoperative TEG maximum amplitude (clot strength) associated with a 5-fold risk of early HAT.
- Unmeasured hypercoagulability attributed to the operating surgeon.
- Intraoperative heparin bolus adopted after hepatic artery anastomosis in selected high-risk recipients.

## TIPS and Portocaval Shunts

- Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) lowers portal hypertension preoperatively.
- May help reduce blood loss.
- Misplaced TIPS can be life-threatening during LT; removal is difficult.
- Temporary portocaval shunts can decompress the portal circulation during hepatectomy.

## Hemostasis During LT

- Infusion of fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate, and antifibrinolytic agents can help.
- Cannot supplant the need for sound surgical technique.
- Good communication with anesthesiology team is essential.
- Scoring systems used to communicate coagulation assessment needs.

## Hyperfibrinolytic State

- Important transition occurs when native liver is removed.
- Recipients develop hyperfibrinolytic state (excessive clot degradation from elevated t-PA).
- After reperfusion, majority of patients correct their fibrinolytic state.
- Rapid clearance of t-PA by the liver (half-life of 5 minutes).

## t-PA Clearance and Antifibrinolytics

- Lack of clearance of t-PA after graft reperfusion associated with massive bleeding.
- Exacerbated by metabolic disturbances.
- Antifibrinolytics may be of value to improve hemostasis control.
- Bleeding may also relate to release of heparin-like substances from the graft.

## Tamponade and Packing

- Protamine administration is rarely used.
- Heparin effect often mediated by plasma transfusion.
- If medical strategies fail, temporary intra-abdominal tamponade with laparotomy packs provides conservative management.
- Temporary vacuum-pack closure with plans for reexploration.
- Packs usually removed within 24 to 48 hours if graft functions well.

## Fibrinolysis Shutdown

- Almost all LT recipients develop inhibition of fibrinolytic system 2 hours after reperfusion.
- Persists beyond postoperative day 1.
- Lack of capacity to break down endogenous clots.
- Essential to not overtransfuse during this time frame.
- Associated with decreased graft survival and postoperative thrombotic complications.

## Postop Transfusion Thresholds

- Decision guided by clinical judgement and stable hemoglobin levels.
- Target hemoglobin of 10 to promote platelet margination.
- Platelet transfusion for absolute count less than 30,000 or TEG MA less than 50 with dropping hemoglobin.
- Plasma for TEG R time greater than 10 mins or INR greater than 2 with dropping hemoglobin.

## Surgical Bleeding Indicators

- Normal coagulation parameters with dropping hemoglobin prompt concerns for surgical bleeding.
- Threshold of more than 6 hours of RBC postoperative bleeding indicates need to return to the OR.

## EAD and PNF: Donor Factors

- Numerous conditions interfere with initial allograft function.
- Donor-related factors:
  - Hemodynamic instability
  - Poor nutritional status
  - Extremes of age
  - Drug toxicity
  - Steatosis

## Primary Nonfunction (PNF)

- Extreme end of graft dysfunction spectrum.
- Requires relisting for transplantation.
- Mortality rate as high as 50% even after re-transplantation.
- Occurs in 2% to 6% of LTs.
- Clinical manifestations: altered mental status, persistent acidosis, hypoglycemia, coagulopathy, hemodynamic instability.

## PNF Risk Factors and Labs

- Major risk factor: steatosis of donor liver.
- Female donor, older donor, long cold/warm ischemia times.
- Labs: serum transaminase levels greater than 8000 IU/L within first 24 to 48 hours.
- Diminished bile and urine output.

## Clinical Assessment of PNF

- Postoperative trends in serum bilirubin and INR are most reliable predictors.
- Should plateau and trend toward normalization.
- Increase portends worse prognosis.
- Resolution of hepatic encephalopathy, adequate urine production, absence of metabolic acidosis are reassuring.
- Metabolic alkalosis may be a sensitive indicator of early graft function (citrate metabolism).

## Early Allograft Dysfunction (EAD)

- Broader term capturing recipients who do not necessarily require re-transplantation but have less favorable outcomes.
- Occurs in roughly 25% of recipients.
- Associated with up to 7-fold increased risk of early graft loss and 10-fold risk of mortality.
- Time frame for diagnosis commonly calculated at 7 days after LT.

## EAD Risk Factors

- High levels of macrosteatosis
- Donor location and weight
- DCD donor
- Recipient obesity and HCC
- Severity of postreperfusion syndrome
- Warm and cold ischemia time
- Operative time
- Amount of transfused fresh frozen plasma

## MEAF Score

- Model for early allograft function (MEAF).
- Continuous variable grading severity of dysfunction.
- Ranges from 1 to 10 based on postoperative day 3 laboratory values.
- Each increase in MEAF score associated with progressively lower graft survival time.

## SFSS in LDLT

- Graft size was an initial concern for EAD.
- Evidence suggests pressure and flow are major contributors rather than size alone.
- Graft to body weight ratio of 0.8 can be transplanted successfully.
- Key prognostic factor: achieving portal systemic gradient less than 15 mm Hg.

## EAD Treatment (Steroids RCT)

- One successful RCT targeting EAD.
- 65 patients randomized to steroids or standard of care (bilirubin greater than 10 on day 7).
- Methylprednisolone IV once daily for 5 days.
- Both arms received oral ursodeoxycholic acid.
- Treatment arm had lower alkaline phosphatase, lower bilirubin, shorter hospital stay.

## Vascular Complications Overview

- Major source of morbidity and graft loss, especially in live-donor grafts.
- Arterial complications account for 64% to 82% of vascular complications.
- Hepatic Artery Thrombosis (HAT) is the most common.

## Hepatic Artery Thrombosis (HAT)

- Overall incidence 1.6% to 8% in adult series.
- 15% to 26% in pediatric patients.
- Incidence in LDLT varies widely.
- Risk factors: CMV positivity, prolonged operating time, redo LT, arterial conduit, variant anatomy, low surgical volume.

## Early vs Late HAT

- Early HAT: time cut off debated (7 to 100 days).
- Late HAT: typically presents as biliary complication or identified incidentally.
- Bilomas are most common presenting symptom of late HAT.
- Late HAT has lower frequency and better prognosis.

## UNOS Policy for Early HAT

- Defines early HAT as lasting less than 7 days.
- Qualifies for status 1A if AST greater than 3000 and INR greater than 2.5 or acidosis.
- Early HAT less than 14 days qualifies recipients as MELD 40.
- Attempt at revascularization should be conducted in early HAT.

## Late HAT Presentation

- Bilomas salvaged with percutaneous drainage and antibiotics.
- Asymptomatic individuals can be followed for biliary complications.
- Risk factors for late HAT: CMV infection and variant arterial anatomy.

## HAT Screening (Doppler US)

- Doppler ultrasound is the best screening method.
- Used liberally in first 2 weeks after transplantation.
- Care must be taken to establish arterial flow within hepatic parenchyma (collateral flow can cause false-negatives).
- Confirmation by celiac arteriography, multiphase CT, or operative exploration.

## Figure 111.1: Hepatic Artery Thrombosis

- Patient experienced rapid increase in serum transaminases early postop.
- Ultrasound could not locate intrahepatic arterial signal.
- Celiac arteriography shows left gastric and splenic arterial flow.
- Fails to show any contrast in the liver.
- Consistent with intimal dissection of the entire common hepatic artery.
- T-tube within the common bile duct is visible.

## Intraoperative HAT Management

- Intimal dissection down to celiac axis is a common cause.
- Immediate reconstruction with donor iliac allograft indicated.
- Patient must not leave OR without completely revascularized graft.
- Autogenous saphenous vein graft used if donor iliac allograft unavailable.
- Artificial conduits (Dacron or ePTFE) rarely used.

## Figure 111.2: Hepatic Artery Reconstruction

- Early diagnosis allows immediate reconstruction.
- Donor iliac artery allograft used.
- Anastomosed between the infrarenal aorta and liver allograft common hepatic artery.

## HAT Clinical Presentation and Treatment

- Ranges from asymptomatic to fulminant hepatic necrosis.
- Common presentation: postoperative biliary complications (leaks, strictures).
- Rapid reestablishment of arterial inflow attempted via urgent operation.
- Thrombolysis and stent placement attempted by some, but durable results limited.
- 50% to 70% ultimately require re-transplantation.

## Portal Vein Thrombosis (PVT) Pre-Surgery

- Previously considered absolute contraindication to OLT.
- Found in 5% to 25% of LT recipients.
- Increases surgical complexity and perioperative morbidity.
- Imaging with duplex or CT before implant is invaluable.

## Yerdel Scoring System for PVT

- Grade 1: less than 50% PVT.
- Grade 2: greater than 50% with minimal SMV obstruction.
- Grade 3: 100% PVT.
- Grade 4: 100% PVT with SMV thrombosis.
- Grades 1 and 2: intraoperative thrombectomy.
- Grade 3: jump graft.
- Grade 4: relative contraindication unless bypass achievable.

## PVT Post-Transplant

- Rare complication, usually technical reasons (incomplete thrombectomy, twisting).
- Early PVT has poor prognosis (50% mortality).
- Risk factors: postop platelet/RBC transfusions, PVT before transplant.
- Late PVT results from intimal hyperplasia with cavernous transformation.
- Treated with angioplasty, stent placement, anticoagulation.

## IVC Obstruction Overview

- Rare complication (1% of patients).
- Piggyback transplantation increasingly popular (donor suprahepatic IVC to recipient middle/left hepatic veins).
- Reduces blood loss, shorter warm ischemia, lower acute kidney injury rates.
- Concerns for increased outflow obstruction due to anastomotic strictures or kinking.

## Outflow Obstruction vs CVP

- Early high outflow obstruction confused with increased central venous pressure (CVP) from high volume resuscitation.
- Nonanatomic source treated with diuretics (target CVP below 11).
- Venography with segmental pressures used if CVP ruled out.
- Gradient greater than 10 mm Hg warrants intervention (angioplasty).

## IVC Thrombosis and VOD/SOS

- IVC thrombosis: direct surgical removal difficult; conservative management with radiologic procedures and anticoagulation preferred.
- Veno-occlusive disease / sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (VOD/SOS).
- Related to acute rejection and drug toxicity.
- Diagnosed via liver biopsy (fibrous obliteration of small hepatic veins).
- TIPS used as last-line therapy.

## Biliary Complications Overview

- Previously considered the "Achilles heel" of LT.
- Improvements in technique reduced complications.
- Obstruction and leaks cause approx. half of all technical failures.
- Require reoperation in 10% to 20% of patients.
- Living-donor grafts have twice the incidence of cadaveric grafts.

## Biliary Leaks Incidence

- Reported incidence varies widely (10% to 50%).
- Most often at choledochal anastomosis or T-tube insertion site.
- Leaks at insertion site observed most frequently at tube removal (25% to 40%).
- Managed conservatively with analgesics and antibiotics.

## T-Tube vs Stenting

- To minimize leak risk, many surgeons prefer not to place stents.
- Alternative: 5 French pediatric feeding tube placed through cystic duct stump.
- Secured with hemorrhoidal band and PDS suture.
- Band obliterates lumen of preformed tract at stent removal (6 to 8 weeks).

## Leak Diagnosis and Management

- Early anastomotic leaks related to technical errors, tension, or ischemic necrosis after HAT.
- Signs: bilious fluid in drains, abdominal/shoulder pain, increased bilirubin, fever.
- Diagnosis: cholangiography, ERC, or PTC.
- ERC favored (endoscopic stent placement without transhepatic catheter risks).
- Large leaks require percutaneous drainage or surgical revision (Roux-en-Y).

## Biliary Strictures Overview

- Occur in approx. 7% to 15% of patients.
- Site of obstruction aids in determining cause.
- Anastomotic stricture accounts for 50% of cases.
- Can occur early (edema) or later (compromised blood supply).

## Anastomotic vs Nonanastomotic

- Anastomotic: usually at the biliary anastomosis.
- Nonanastomotic obstruction (NAS): caused by bile duct ischemia or sludge/debris.
- NAS can occur in hilar region or intrahepatically.
- Suspect thrombosis of hepatic artery or branches.

## Figure 111.3: Biliary Stricture

- Patient with previously created Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy.
- Now has an anastomotic stricture.
- Note the dilated intrahepatic ducts.
- Percutaneous access of the Roux-en-Y limb affords diagnosis and treatment with balloon dilation.
- Avoids placement of transhepatic catheters.

## Stricture Risk Factors

- Technical error during reconstruction.
- ABO incompatibility.
- Prolonged preservation times.
- Recurrent rejection.
- Viral infections.
- Recurrence of primary ductal disease (up to 50% at long-term follow-up).

## NAS in LDLT and DCD

- Anastomotic leak or stricture twice more common after LDLT vs cadaveric LT.
- NAS associated with chronic ductopenic rejection, ABO incompatibility.
- Ischemia-reperfusion injury associated with allograft preservation.
- Especially common in grafts from DCD donors.

## Figure 111.4: Nonanastomotic Stricture

- Nonanastomotic biliary stricture observed from ischemic injury.
- Liver graft from a donor who died of cardiac death (DCD).
- DCD grafts are more prone to ischemic injury problems such as bile duct stricture.

## Stricture Treatment

- ERC recommended to confirm diagnosis and implement immediate stenting.
- Failure to cross stricture endoscopically requires PTC or surgical revision (Roux-en-Y).
- Intrahepatic strictures best treated with percutaneous balloon dilation.
- Long-term stents rarely needed.

## Ischemic Cholangiopathy Overview

- Spectrum of NAS that tends to be diffuse.
- Main causes: ischemia reperfusion injury, immune mediated injury, bile salt injury.
- Major risk factors: HAT and DCD donors.
- Clinical vs subclinical cholangiopathy.
- Rapidly progressive form associated with necrosis warrants urgent re-transplantation.

## Ischemic Cholangiopathy Prevention

- Best strategy is avoidance.
- tPA treatment in DCD donors reduces ischemic cholangiopathy and improves graft survival.
- Machine perfusion of high-risk donors shows promising results in reducing biliary complications.

## Renal Dysfunction Overview

- Observed to some degree in almost every LT patient.
- Early dysfunction: oliguria with transient creatinine increase, or anuria with acute renal failure.
- Risk factors: preexisting renal dysfunction, primary graft nonfunction.
- Usual mechanism: prerenal azotemia secondary to hypotension/hypovolemia.

## CNI Toxicity

- Calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine and tacrolimus) are nephrotoxic.
- Renal failure induced by CNIs occurs in approx. 5% of patients.
- Long-term exposure is a clear risk factor.
- Interest in automatic dose reduction or substitution with mTOR inhibitors.

## mTOR Inhibitors (Sirolimus)

- Macrocyclic antibiotic used for renal sparing.
- Disadvantages: dyslipidemia, impaired wound healing (alterations in VEGF).
- Apparent benefit in reducing cancer formation.
- Associated with early HAT; wait at least 4 weeks post-transplant before initiating.

## Fluid and Electrolyte Disturbances

- Universal after LT.
- Preoperative malnutrition and ESLD lead to derangements in total body water and electrolytes.
- Worsened by metabolic stress of surgery and massive resuscitation.
- Recovery depends on renal and liver allograft function.

## Metabolic Alkalosis

- Early development secondary to metabolism of citrate in blood products.
- Favorable sign of graft function.
- Serious if alkalemia develops.
- Judicious replacement of chloride (normal saline or hydrogen chloride) warranted.

## Acute Cellular Rejection Overview

- Acute deterioration in allograft function with specific histologic changes.
- Mixed inflammatory cell infiltrate (predominantly lymphocytes).
- Involves portal triads, disrupts biliary, hepatic artery, and portal venous endothelia.
- Incidence approx. 45%.

## Rejection Clinical Signs

- Early stage: mostly asymptomatic.
- Signs: fever, abdominal pain, malaise, fatigue, poor appetite.
- Earliest lab indicator: elevated bilirubin.
- Modest increase in alkaline phosphatase and transaminases.
- PT and serum albumin usually unaffected.

## Rejection Diagnosis (Banff)

- Lab measurements neither sensitive nor specific.
- Liver histology from percutaneous biopsy is the standard.
- Banff score used for evaluation:
  - Mild (RAI less than 4)
  - Moderate (RAI 4 to 6)
  - Severe (RAI greater than 7)

## Rejection Treatment

- Mild: increasing calcineurin inhibitor.
- Moderate and severe: high-dose pulse corticosteroids (successful in 80% to 90% of cases).
- Antithymocyte globulin (thymoglobulin) does not improve rates as induction agent.
- Can be used as adjunct in steroid-resistant antibody-mediated rejection (AMR).

## Chronic Rejection

- Associated with reduced graft survival.
- Occurs in roughly 10% of all LTs.
- No effective treatments.
- Ductopenic rejection: loss of bile ducts in more than 50% of portal tracts.
- Arteriopathy affects large and medium-sized arteries.
- Only effective treatment is re-transplantation.

## Antibody-Mediated Rejection (AMR)

- Rare form of immunologic complication (1% of all LTs).
- Increased to 5% in patients with positive donor-specific antigen (DSA).
- Diagnosed with C4D-positive stained biopsies.
- Treatment: plasmapheresis, IVIG, rituximab.
- Rising DSA post-transplant could cause occult liver fibrosis.

## Infection Overview

- Lifelong immunosuppressant therapy required.
- Tenuous balance between preventing rejection and minimizing infection/PTLD risk.
- Two-thirds of transplant patients experience at least one serious infection.
- Accounts for more than half of observed mortality associated with LT.

## Bacterial Infections

- Tend to occur within first month.
- Risk factors: prolonged operating time, indwelling catheters, biliary obstruction, PVT, poor graft function.
- Common pathogens: gram-negative (E. coli, Enterobacter, Pseudomonas) and gram-positive (S. aureus, coagulase-negative staph).
- Rarely, S. aureus causes toxic shock syndrome.

## Viral Infections Overview

- Common in immunocompromised patients.
- Includes HIV, adenovirus, influenza, RSV.
- Risk of acquiring viral hepatitis from infected organs, blood, or illicit drug use.
- CMV is the most important infection in organ transplant patients.

## CMV Disease vs Infection

- CMV disease usually occurs 30 to 50 days post-transplant.
- Manifestations: fever, malaise, arthralgia, leukopenia, hepatitis, pneumonitis, enterocolitis.
- CMV disease: histologically evident invasive infection or positive culture from deep tissue.
- Positive blood/serologic tests insufficient for disease diagnosis.

## CMV Histology and Risk Factors

- Liver biopsy with immunostaining enables early diagnosis.
- Histology: hepatocyte necrosis, parenchymal microabscesses, magenta-colored intranuclear inclusion (owl's eye nucleus).
- Risk factors: seronegative recipient / seropositive donor, anti-lymphocyte antibody therapy, re-transplantation.
- Chronic CMV associated with cholestatic hepatitis and vanishing bile duct syndrome.

## CMV Treatment and Prophylaxis

- Reduce immunosuppressive regimen if possible.
- IV ganciclovir mainstay of therapy.
- Foscarnet alternative (nephrotoxic).
- Oral valganciclovir effective for prevention and mild infection.
- Prophylactic regimens range from 3 to 6 months of daily oral treatment.

## HSV and EBV

- HSV seropositivity present in most patients.
- Postop infection usually reactivation due to immunosuppression.
- Mild mucocutaneous disease responds to acyclovir.
- EBV infection characterized by mononucleosis-like syndrome.
- Clinical significance: pathogenesis of PTLD (unrestricted B cell proliferation).

## Fungal Infections Overview

- Clinically significant fungal infection incidence: 20% to 25%.
- Risk factors: poor nutrition, re-transplantation, prolonged antibiotics, high immunosuppression, Roux-en-Y.
- Invasive fungal infection: 1% to 3% incidence, high mortality.
- Prophylactic antifungals reduce postoperative invasive fungal infections.

## Candida and Aspergillus

- Candida: most common fungal infection.
- Aspergillus: second most frequent, angioinvasive, disseminates to CNS and lungs.
- Invasive aspergillosis incidence approx. 1%, mortality close to 100% despite treatment.

## Cryptococcus and Coccidiomycosis

- Cryptococcus neoformans: occurs months to years post-transplant (0.25%).
- Subtle signs: mental status changes, headache, fever.
- Coccidiomycosis: rare, endemic to southwest.
- Long-term fluconazole prophylaxis given to recipients from this region.

## P. carinii and Legionella

- Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia decreased dramatically with routine TMP/SMX prophylaxis.
- Occurs almost exclusively in patients without prophylaxis.
- Legionella pneumophila: uncommon cause of pneumonia.
- Source usually water supply.
- Treated with quinolones (do not interact with CNIs).

## PTLD Overview

- Life-threatening complication of chronic immunosuppression.
- Strongly associated with EBV replication in B cells.
- Incidence 1% to 3% among LT recipients.
- Polyclonal PTLD: treatable with discontinuation of immunosuppression.
- Monoclonal PTLD: difficult to treat, can result in death.

## PTLD Treatment

- Clinical presentation: fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy, GI bleeding/perforation, CNS manifestations.
- Non-Hodgkin lymphoma accounts for 93% of lymphomas in transplant recipients.
- Extranodal involvement common (70%).
- Monoclonal antibody against CD20 (rituximab) shows promising results.

## Immunosuppressive Toxicity

- CNIs (cyclosporine, tacrolimus) side effects: GI disturbances, headache, tremor.
- Cyclosporine: gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism.
- Tacrolimus: glucose intolerance.
- Renal tubular dysfunction: hyperkalemia, hyperuricemia, hypophosphatemia, hypomagnesemia.
- Nephrotoxicity is most clinically significant adverse effect.

## Mycophenolate Mofetil

- Side effects: GI disturbances (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea).
- May increase certain postoperative infections.
- Difficult to differentiate from early transplant symptoms.
- Alternative forms, dose modification, or discontinuation may help.

## Recurrent Hepatitis (HBV and HCV)

- HBV: recurrence rate 80% to 90% in first year without prophylaxis.
- HBIG and adjuvant therapies (lamivudine) allow routine transplantation with excellent results.
- HCV: recurrent infection universal (90% confirmed on biopsy).
- Improved HCV medications with almost 100% cure rates significantly improve outlook.

## Bone Disease

- Hepatic osteodystrophy in almost all patients (especially primary biliary cirrhosis).
- Causes: corticosteroid therapy, bed rest, cholestasis.
- Osteoporosis common 3 to 6 months post-LT.
- Bone density starts gaining by end of first year.
- Atraumatic fractures frequent within first 6 months.

## Neuropsychiatric Complications

- Severe changes can occur.
- Anxiety and depression common.
- Seizures, altered consciousness, CNS infections infrequent but significant.
- Encephalopathy often multifactorial (metabolic, hypoxia, sedation, drugs).
- CNI toxicity: tremors, headaches, seizures (avoid by monitoring drug levels).

## Hypertension and Hyperlipidemia

- Common sequelae of immunosuppression.
- Hypertension observed in approx. 70% at 1 year.
- 40% manifest metabolic syndrome (diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, hypertriglyceridemia).
- Rapamycin causes hyperlipidemia and wound healing issues.
- Omega-3 fatty acids (fish oil) reduce hypertriglyceridemia significantly.

## Conclusion

- LT is a lifesaving treatment for ESLD.
- Preoperative comorbidities contribute to postoperative complications.
- Aggressive immunosuppression prevents rejection but risks neoplasms/infections.
- Trend toward significant reduction of immunosuppression and early steroid withdrawal.
- Multidisciplinary team approach essential for constant surveillance and early diagnosis.
